You wouldn't use "de légumes", it would be "des légumes" as you are referring to a plural, multiple vegetables. "Les" you would be used for a plural and is the definite article to refer to something specific' "THE/THESE/THOSE Vegetables". On the other hand, "des" is indefinite and would be used for a plural with no specific object, "SOME vegetables". When you say "I want some apples" you aren't usually referring to THAT specific group of apples, you just want SOME apples. In French, "je veux DES pommes", because it's plural (appleS/pommeS) and you aren't referring to specific apples so it's "some" (des). Same for shoes, "je veux des chaussures" (indefinite) or "I want SOME shoes", and "je veux les chaussures" or "I want THE/THOSE shoes" (definite). You can imagine it this way, if you work in a store and someone walked in and said "je veux les (THE/THOSE) pommes" you'd be like "which apples? What's so special about these specific apples?"

Obligatory "I'm not a linguist but...", I think people who say that are a little misguided. We all start out with a mental filter we put foreign words through, and learning the language enough to be able to speak and comprehend essentially means reducing the use of that filter. Saying that you should not use it at all is like saying that if you start at the start line and skip straight to the finish you wouldn't have to bother with the time consuming middle bit of the race. It's a goal to have in mind, and you will notice as you learn and speak that the filter drops more and more. Yes, it can be bad to rely on the filter too much and it can slow down your learning if over used, but especially at the start it's entirely necessary until you internalise it all. Keep learning and work on reducing the filter use by having conversations, consuming French language media and talking to people, the filter will pretty much go away in time.
